questions.title: Abstract Shape Area Calculation
questions.question: Write an abstract class Shape with an abstract method area(), and create concrete subclasses Circle and Rectangle that implement it.
questions.explanation: An abstract class serves as an incomplete blueprint that cannot be instantiated directly with the new operator. By declaring an abstract method like double area(), the base class defines an interface contract while omitting implementation details. Subclasses extending Shape must provide concrete method bodies for area() by implementing formulas such as pi*r*r and width*height. At runtime, calling area() on a Shape reference relies on dynamic method dispatch to execute the subclass implementation.
hints: Declare the base class using the abstract keyword: public abstract class Shape.
Define the method without a body: public abstract double area();.
Override area() in Circle and Rectangle with appropriate geometric formulas.

questions.title: Drawable Interface Implementation
questions.question: Write an interface Drawable with a draw() method and implement it across two separate classes, Circle and Rectangle.
questions.explanation: An interface in Java establishes a behavioral contract consisting of abstract methods that implementing classes must satisfy. Unlike class inheritance, a class can implement multiple interfaces, enabling flexible polymorphic behavior. Methods in an interface are implicitly public and abstract. When Circle and Rectangle declare implements Drawable, both agree to provide public implementations of draw(). Invoking draw() through a Drawable reference dispatches to the corresponding concrete class implementation via the invokeinterface bytecode instruction.
hints: Declare the interface with void draw(); without method bodies.
Use the implements keyword in Circle and Rectangle.
Ensure the draw() implementation method is marked with public visibility.
questions.expectedOutput:
Circle is drawing
Rectangle is drawing

questions.title: Abstract and Concrete Method Hybrid
questions.question: Write an abstract class containing both an abstract method and a concrete method, and invoke both methods through a subclass instance.
questions.explanation: Abstract classes allow mixing fully implemented concrete methods with unpopulated abstract methods. Concrete methods provide shared, reusable functionality across all subclasses, preventing code duplication. Abstract methods define extension points where each subclass must provide specialized logic. When a subclass extends the abstract class, it inherits the concrete methods directly and implements the abstract ones. Calling both demonstrates how abstract base classes combine shared behavior with custom extension points.
hints: Include at least one method with a body and one method ending with a semicolon marked abstract.
Extend the abstract class in a subclass and implement the abstract method.
Call both inherited concrete and overridden abstract methods on the subclass instance.

questions.title: Interface Default Method Overriding
questions.question: Write an interface with a default method, implement it in two classes, and override the default method in one implementation.
questions.explanation: Default methods, introduced in Java 8, permit interfaces to define method implementations using the default modifier. This enables interface evolution by allowing new methods to be added to existing interfaces without breaking backward compatibility for implementing classes. Implementing classes can inherit the default implementation directly or override it with customized behavior. When overridden, the subclass method replaces the interface's default fallback logic during dynamic dispatch.
hints: Declare a method using the default keyword inside the interface.
Provide a concrete block body for the default method.
In one class, inherit the default method as-is; in the second class, override it with custom logic.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent method called
Child method called

questions.title: Abstract Animal Class with Template Call
questions.question: Write an abstract class Animal with an abstract sound() method and a concrete describe() method that invokes sound().
questions.explanation: Concrete methods inside an abstract class can invoke abstract methods declared within the same class. During compilation, the compiler permits calls to abstract methods because it guarantees that any instantiable subclass will provide a concrete implementation. When describe() runs on a Dog instance, calling sound() resolves via dynamic method dispatch to Dog.sound(). This pattern demonstrates how abstract classes can coordinate workflows that incorporate specialized subclass logic.
hints: Declare public abstract String sound(); in the Animal class.
Implement public void describe() to format and print the result of sound().
Override sound() in a subclass to supply the specific text.

questions.title: Concrete Formatting Wrapper in Abstract Class
questions.question: Add a concrete method void display() to an abstract class that formats and prints the output of an abstract calculation method implemented by a subclass.
questions.explanation: Centralizing output presentation in a base class while delegating calculation steps to subclasses keeps code organized and maintainable. In the abstract class Measurement, display() formats and outputs values returned by the abstract computeMetric() method. Subclasses implement the calculation logic without needing to duplicate string formatting or printing logic. This separation keeps presentation rules consistent across all measurement implementations.
hints: Define public abstract int computeMetric(); in the abstract class.
Define public void display() in the abstract class to print formatted output using computeMetric().
Extend with a concrete subclass that implements computeMetric().

questions.title: Abstract Method Contract Fulfillment
questions.question: Demonstrate that a non-abstract subclass must implement all inherited abstract methods from its base class to compile successfully.
questions.explanation: Abstract methods define required contracts that concrete subclasses must satisfy. If a subclass extends an abstract class but fails to implement even one inherited abstract method, the compiler generates an error: 'Class is not abstract and does not override abstract method'. To compile, the subclass must either provide concrete method bodies for all abstract methods or be declared abstract itself. Providing concrete implementations for all abstract methods fulfills the contract and allows the class to be instantiated.
hints: Declare two abstract methods in the base class: stepA() and stepB().
Override both methods in the concrete subclass with working implementations.
Note that leaving either method unimplemented triggers a compile-time error.

questions.title: Abstract Class Reference Polymorphism
questions.question: Declare a variable of an abstract class type, assign a concrete subclass instance to it, and demonstrate polymorphic method dispatch.
questions.explanation: Although abstract classes cannot be instantiated with new, they serve as valid reference types that can hold references to instances of any concrete subclass. In BaseService service = new CustomService(), the variable type is BaseService, but the runtime object on the heap is CustomService. When an overridden method is called, the JVM uses dynamic method dispatch (invokevirtual) to invoke the subclass implementation. This allows programs to work with generic base types while executing specialized subclass behavior at runtime.
hints: Declare the reference variable with the abstract class type.
Instantiate the concrete subclass using new ConcreteSubclass().
Invoke the overridden method to observe dynamic runtime dispatch.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent method called
Child method called

questions.title: Abstract Class Constructor and State Chaining
questions.question: Write an abstract class with a parameterized constructor that initializes private member fields, and invoke it from a subclass constructor using super().
questions.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated on their own, but they can define constructors to initialize base state. When a concrete subclass is instantiated, its constructor must call a superclass constructor as its first statement, either implicitly or explicitly via super(...). This ensures that fields declared in the abstract base class are properly initialized before subclass initialization logic runs. Defining constructors in abstract classes allows base invariants to be enforced across all subclasses without duplicating initialization logic.
hints: Define an explicit constructor in the abstract class accepting initialization arguments.
In the subclass constructor, call super(args) as the first statement.
Access the initialized base field in subclass methods using protected access or a getter.

questions.title: Polymorphic Interface List Processing
questions.question: Implement an interface across three distinct classes, store instances of each in a List of the interface type, and iterate over the collection to invoke methods polymorphically.
questions.explanation: Using interfaces as collection element types decouples collection management from specific class implementations. When TaskA, TaskB, and TaskC all implement Task, instances of each can be added to a shared List<Task>. In an enhanced for-loop, calling task.run() uses interface method dispatch (invokeinterface) to execute the corresponding subclass implementation. This allows adding new task types to the collection without modifying the loop that processes them.
hints: Declare a common interface: interface Task { void run(); }.
Implement Task across three separate classes.
Populate a List<Task> and iterate over it using an enhanced for-loop.
questions.expectedOutput:
Task A completed
Task B completed
Task C completed

questions.title: Abstract Payment Processing Architecture
questions.question: Build an extensible payment system using an abstract class PaymentMethod with concrete subclasses CreditCard, UPI, and Cash that implement transaction processing.
questions.explanation: Payment systems require standardized processing workflows alongside payment-specific execution logic. The abstract base class PaymentMethod encapsulates common attributes like the transaction amount and declares an abstract method processPayment(). Subclasses like CreditCard, UPI, and Cash extend the base class and implement their respective payment mechanisms. This architecture makes it straightforward to add new payment methods without modifying checkout logic that operates against the base PaymentMethod type.
hints: Store the payment amount in PaymentMethod and initialize it via super(amount).
Declare public abstract void processPayment(); in the base class.
Implement processPayment() in CreditCard, UPI, and Cash with channel-specific output.
questions.expectedOutput:
Paying 100.0 using Credit Card
Paying 100.0 using UPI
Paying 100.0 using Cash

questions.title: Static Methods and Constants in Interfaces
questions.question: Write an interface containing a constant field and a static method, and demonstrate accessing both directly without instantiating an implementing class.
questions.explanation: Interfaces can define both static methods and constant fields alongside abstract methods. Any field declared inside an interface is implicitly public static final, serving as a compile-time constant. Static methods in interfaces, introduced in Java 8, provide utility logic tied directly to the interface contract without requiring a separate utility class. Interface static methods do not participate in inheritance and cannot be overridden by implementing classes; they must be invoked directly using the interface name.
hints: Declare a constant field in the interface: String REGISTRY_TAG = "APP_2026";.
Declare a static method in the interface: static void printInfo() { ... }.
Call the static method directly using InterfaceName.methodName().

questions.title: Partial Implementation via Intermediate Abstract Class
questions.question: Write an abstract class that implements an interface partially, leaving the remaining methods for a concrete subclass to complete.
questions.explanation: When an abstract class implements an interface, it is not required to provide method bodies for all declared interface methods. The abstract class can implement a subset of methods to provide shared foundational behavior, while leaving the remaining methods abstract. A concrete subclass that extends the abstract class must then implement the remaining interface methods to complete the contract. This design pattern reduces boilerplate by providing default plumbing while leaving domain-specific methods open for implementation.
hints: Define an interface with two methods: init() and execute().
Implement init() in the abstract class, leaving execute() unimplemented.
Extend the abstract class with a concrete subclass that implements execute().

questions.title: Template Method Data Mining Pattern
questions.question: Create an abstract DataMiner class implementing a final void mine() template method that coordinates abstract steps openFile(), extractData(), and closeFile().
questions.explanation: The Template Method design pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class method while allowing subclasses to override specific steps without changing the overall structure. In DataMiner, the method public final void mine() coordinates the sequence: openFile(), extractData(), and closeFile(). Marking the template method final prevents subclasses from altering the execution order. Subclasses supply specific implementations for the abstract hook methods, ensuring the overall workflow remains intact across formats.
hints: Declare public final void mine() in DataMiner to lock down the execution order.
Define abstract methods for openFile(), extractData(), and closeFile().
Extend with a concrete subclass that implements the steps, and call mine().

questions.title: Tiered Vehicle Abstraction Hierarchy
questions.question: Create an abstract class Vehicle, an intermediate abstract class MotorizedVehicle that implements motor initialization, and a concrete subclass Car that implements steering.
questions.explanation: Complex domain models often layer abstraction across multiple levels of inheritance. The root abstract class Vehicle establishes the core contract (start(), steer()). The intermediate abstract class MotorizedVehicle implements start() with engine-specific logic while leaving specialized methods like steer() abstract. The concrete subclass Car completes the chain by implementing the remaining abstract methods. This multi-tier hierarchy allows intermediate classes to add shared functionality progressively, reducing boilerplate in leaf classes.
hints: Root class Vehicle declares abstract void start(); and abstract void steer();.
Intermediate class MotorizedVehicle implements start() and leaves steer() abstract.
Concrete class Car implements steer().

questions.title: Interface Contract with Abstract Base Class State
questions.question: Build an architecture combining an interface Payable with an abstract base class BaseEmployee implementing shared state, extended by HourlyEmployee.
questions.explanation: Combining interfaces and abstract classes leverages the strengths of both abstractions. The interface Payable defines a contract (processPayment()) that can be implemented by any billable entity. The abstract class BaseEmployee implements Payable and encapsulates shared employee state (such as name), saving subclasses from re-declaring common fields. The concrete subclass HourlyEmployee extends BaseEmployee and implements the pay processing logic. This pattern provides broad contract compatibility via the interface while enabling internal state and code reuse via the abstract base class.
hints: Declare interface Payable with void processPayment();.
Create abstract class BaseEmployee implements Payable to store shared employee fields.
Extend BaseEmployee with HourlyEmployee and implement processPayment().

questions.title: Static and Final Modifiers in Abstract Classes
questions.question: Demonstrate that an abstract class can contain static methods, static fields, and final methods, but cannot be declared final itself.
questions.explanation: Abstract classes have distinct rules regarding static and final modifiers. An abstract class cannot be marked final because final prevents inheritance, while abstract requires inheritance, making final abstract a contradictory compile-time error. However, within an abstract class, individual methods can be marked final to prevent subclasses from overriding them. Abstract classes can also declare static fields and static utility methods that can be called directly via the class name without instantiation. This exercise illustrates how these modifiers interact within abstract class definitions.
hints: Declare a static utility method and a static field inside the abstract class.
Include a final concrete method inside the abstract class.
Extend with a subclass, call the inherited final method, and invoke the static method directly.

questions.title: Abstract Event Processing Lifecycle Pipeline
questions.question: Design an abstract EventHandler pipeline with lifecycle hooks beforeHandle(), an abstract handle(), and afterHandle().
questions.explanation: Event processing pipelines often wrap core execution logic with pre- and post-processing steps. The abstract class EventHandler defines a template method dispatch() that coordinates the sequence: beforeHandle(), handle(), and afterHandle(). Default hook implementations in the base class provide standard behavior, while subclasses override handle() to implement event-specific processing. Subclasses can also optionally override the hooks to add custom behavior before or after execution, demonstrating flexible event pipeline design.
hints: Provide default implementations for beforeHandle() and afterHandle() in the abstract class.
Declare abstract void handle(); to enforce custom handling logic in subclasses.
Orchestrate all three calls in a dispatch() method.

questions.title: Data Pipeline Template Method Pattern
questions.question: Implement the Template Method pattern using an abstract DataProcessor with a final process() method coordinating readData(), transform(), and writeData().
questions.explanation: Data processing engines use the Template Method pattern to enforce a consistent pipeline while supporting different data sources and formats. The abstract class DataProcessor defines the overarching workflow in public final void process(): reading input, applying transformations, and writing output. Marking process() as final ensures subclasses cannot alter the processing order. Subclasses implement the abstract steps (readData, transform, writeData) for specific targets (e.g., JSON, CSV, databases). This separates pipeline structure from format-specific parsing logic.
hints: Mark the main process() pipeline method final to prevent override tampering.
Define abstract protected methods: readData(), transform(), and writeData().
Implement a concrete pipeline subclass and invoke process() to verify execution order.

questions.title: Strategy Design Pattern via Functional Interfaces
questions.question: Implement the Strategy pattern using a functional interface SortStrategy, supplying sorting implementations using lambda expressions.
questions.explanation: The Strategy pattern decouples an algorithm from the context that uses it, allowing algorithms to be swapped at runtime. In modern Java, a single-method interface decorated with @FunctionalInterface acts as a Strategy abstraction. Instead of creating verbose subclasses, callers can pass sorting algorithms as lambda expressions or method references. The context class accepts the SortStrategy via dependency injection and executes it without being coupled to a specific sorting implementation.
hints: Define @FunctionalInterface interface SortStrategy { void sort(int[] arr); }.
Implement an execution context class that accepts a SortStrategy parameter.
Pass a lambda expression implementing the sorting algorithm into the context.

questions.title: Interface Default Method Conflict Resolution
questions.question: Create two interfaces defining conflicting default methods with the exact same signature, implement both in a single class, and resolve the ambiguity using InterfaceName.super.method().
questions.explanation: When a class implements multiple interfaces that define default methods with the same signature, Java faces a diamond conflict. Because the compiler cannot determine which default implementation to prefer, it raises an error: 'class inherits unrelated defaults for method()'. The implementing class must resolve the ambiguity by explicitly overriding the conflicting method. Inside the overridden method, the developer can provide custom logic or explicitly delegate to one of the interface implementations using InterfaceName.super.method().
hints: Declare default void ping() in two separate interfaces (e.g., Alpha and Beta).
Override ping() in the implementing class to satisfy the compiler.
Use Alpha.super.ping() to explicitly invoke the desired interface implementation.

questions.title: Polymorphic Plugin Multi-Form Instantiation
questions.question: Design a Plugin interface and demonstrate loading multiple implementations—a standard class and a lambda expression—into a shared list to execute polymorphically.
questions.explanation: Extensible plugin architectures rely on interfaces to decouple the host application from extension logic. This exercise demonstrates multiple ways to instantiate interface types in Java: declaring a standard concrete class and defining a concise lambda expression. Both approaches produce instances that satisfy the Plugin contract, allowing them to be stored in a common List<Plugin> and executed polymorphically through a unified loop.
hints: Define @FunctionalInterface interface Plugin { void run(); }.
Add a concrete class instance and a lambda () -> ... into a List<Plugin>.
Iterate over the list and invoke run() on each plugin.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent method called
Child method called

questions.title: Segregated Notification Architecture
questions.question: Design a notification system combining an abstract Notification base class for core delivery with an optional Retryable interface for channels supporting retries.
questions.explanation: Following the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP), classes should not be forced to implement contracts they do not support. In this design, the abstract base class Notification encapsulates shared fields (recipient) and defines an abstract send() method. Because not all notification channels support retries (e.g., standard SMS vs. persistent MQ channels), retry functionality is separated into an independent Retryable interface. Channels that support retries implement Retryable, while others extend only Notification. Processing loops can then inspect for retry capabilities using instanceof without polluting the base class.
hints: Create an abstract class Notification with abstract void send();.
Create an interface Retryable with void retry();.
Extend Notification and implement Retryable in a specialized subclass.

questions.title: Sealed Abstract Expression Hierarchy
questions.question: Implement an algebraic expression tree using a sealed abstract class Expression that permits only Constant and BinaryOp subclasses.
questions.explanation: Introduced in Java 17, sealed classes allow developers to restrict which subclasses can extend a class. Declaring sealed abstract class Expression permits Constant, BinaryOp tells the compiler to prevent any other class from extending Expression. This gives library designers control over class hierarchies, which is useful when modeling closed algebraic domains or ASTs. Because the compiler knows all possible subclasses at compile time, it can verify that pattern-matching switch expressions over the hierarchy are exhaustive without needing a default case.
hints: Use sealed abstract class Expression permits Constant, BinaryOp.
Mark the permitted subclasses final: final class Constant extends Expression.
Implement an abstract eval() method across the hierarchy.

questions.title: F-Bounded Polymorphic Entity Comparison
questions.question: Design an abstract base class using F-bounded polymorphism abstract class ComparableEntity<T extends ComparableEntity<T>> to enforce type-safe comparison methods.
questions.explanation: F-bounded polymorphism (self-referential generics) allows an abstract base class to refer to its concrete subclass in its generic signature: abstract class Entity<T extends Entity<T>>. This pattern is used in core APIs like Comparable<T> and Enum<E extends Enum<E>>. It ensures that comparison or builder methods work strictly with the matching subclass type rather than the base class. For example, extending Entity<Account> guarantees that an Account can only be compared against another Account, catching mismatched cross-entity comparisons at compile time.
hints: Define the class bound as abstract class ComparableEntity<T extends ComparableEntity<T>>.
Declare public abstract boolean isSame(T other); using the generic type T.
Extend using class User extends ComparableEntity<User> to bind the self-referential generic.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent method called
Child method called

questions.title: Abstract Generic Data Access Layer (DAO)
questions.question: Implement an abstract generic DAO (AbstractDao<T, ID>) that provides template CRUD methods while delegating persistence operations to abstract storage hooks.
questions.explanation: Enterprise persistence architectures often use an abstract generic Data Access Object (DAO) to centralize CRUD workflows while keeping storage implementations pluggable. AbstractDao<T, ID> coordinates operations like save(T entity): it runs validation, calls the abstract hook persist(entity), and logs the event. Concrete DAOs supply the storage-specific logic (in-memory, SQL, or NoSQL) by implementing the hook. This separates validation and transaction coordination from physical database operations.
hints: Declare the abstract class with type parameters: AbstractDao<T, ID>.
Implement a concrete public final void save(T entity) that calls protected abstract void doPersist(T entity).
Implement a concrete subclass like UserDao to provide the storage hook.

questions.title: Pluggable Filter Chain Architecture
questions.question: Build an abstract packet processing filter chain where an AbstractFilter manages link pointers to subsequent filters and invokes an abstract filter(Packet p) hook.
questions.explanation: The Chain of Responsibility design pattern coordinates a pipeline of handlers. The abstract base class AbstractFilter encapsulates a reference to the next filter in the sequence (nextFilter). When process(Packet p) executes, it runs the abstract transformation method filter(p) and then forwards the packet to nextFilter.process(p) if one exists. Concrete filters implement specific checks (like authentication or payload decoding) without managing chain traversal themselves, enabling modular, reconfigurable processing pipelines.
hints: Include a private AbstractFilter next; field and a public linkWith(AbstractFilter next) method.
Implement public void process(String data) calling abstract filter(data) before delegating to next.
Link concrete filter implementations together and execute the chain.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent method called
Child method called

questions.title: Workflow Orchestration Engine
questions.question: Implement an abstract workflow engine that coordinates multi-step business transactions, handles rollbacks on failure, and manages execution via abstract lifecycle hooks.
questions.explanation: Enterprise workflow engines use abstraction to coordinate multi-step transactions that require compensation (rollback) logic on failure. The abstract class WorkflowEngine defines a template method runWorkflow(): it executes steps sequentially and calls rollback() if an exception occurs. Concrete workflows implement the abstract business steps (stepOne(), stepTwo(), and rollback()). Centralizing error handling and compensation in the abstract engine ensures transaction workflows fail safely without leaving the system in an inconsistent state.
hints: Implement public final void runWorkflow() inside a try-catch block.
Call stepOne() and stepTwo() in the try block, and call rollback() in the catch block.
Implement the steps in a concrete workflow subclass.
